name: Mexico
card_headline: Homicides are down about half on official figures, but 130,000 people are missing, Washington ties tariffs to security, and the USMCA faces yearly reviews.
card_summary: The Security Cabinet says daily homicides fell 52 percent in two years, though the figure compares two months and is disputed. Official records list more than 130,000 people as missing. The Sinaloa cartel war continues, and the army killed CJNG leader El Mencho in February. The US indicted Sinaloa's governor in April and declined in July to renew the USMCA. Sheinbaum and Trump meet again at the G20 in Florida in December. Judges are now elected, and the second vote moved to 2028.
card_local: Animal Político, Proceso and Ríodoce report on missing people, graves in Mexico City, forced recruitment and the Sinaloa toll, and UnoTV's weekly registry count shows 217 new cases for 9 to 15 November. [1] [2] [3] [4]
card_international: Reuters reports that Sheinbaum hopes to close a trade deal with Trump at the G20, and AP reports that Mexico is receiving third-country deportees. [5] [6]
card_scholar: WOLA argues the killing of El Mencho shows the limits of the kingpin strategy, and CSIS says trade and security are now fused in US demands. [7] [8]
context_md: Claudia Sheinbaum has governed since October 2024. [9] The Sinaloa Cartel has been fractured since the arrest of El Mayo that year, with the Chapitos and Mayitos fighting each other. [9] A constitutional reform that took effect on 16 September 2024 made judges elected officials. [10] A UNAM researcher writes that Morena has a constitutional majority, though allied parties broke ranks on the March 2026 electoral bill. [11] The United States has designated Mexican criminal groups as terrorist organisations, which Mexico rejects as a label. [12] Mexico was the top US trading partner in 2024, with nearly US$930 billion in total trade. [13] Official records list more than 132,000 people as missing. [14]

sections.title: Homicides are down about half on the government's count, and Sinaloa is the main exception
sections.body_md:
The Security Cabinet says the daily average of intentional homicides fell 52 percent in two years. [15] Press reporting on the national statistics secretariat's figures gives 43.4 a day in October 2026 against 86.9 in September 2024, which compares two single months. [16] Government data also show seven states produced 49.3 percent of homicides from January to August 2026: Guanajuato, Baja California, Chihuahua, Sinaloa, the State of Mexico, Guerrero and Morelos. [17]

The explanation is contested. Analyst Andrés Sumano of El Colef told EFE there is no single cause. He points to government action, changes in how deaths are recorded and the reorganisation of crime, and says that when one group monopolises a territory the competition behind killings disappears. The opposition PAN, through Ricardo Anaya, accuses the government of manipulating statistics. [17]

Sinaloa shows what the national average hides. Animal Político counted 2,425 intentional homicides in the first 17 months of the Chapitos versus Mayiza fight, and the newspaper Noroeste counted 166 violent deaths in December 2025 against the state prosecutor's 128. [18] Ríodoce, drawing on the Institute for Economics and Peace, reports that Culiacán's homicide rate rose from 64 to 107 per 100,000 between 2024 and 2025 and that Sinaloa ranked second-least peaceful among states. [3]

On 22 February army special forces located Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) leader Nemesio Oseguera, known as El Mencho, in Tapalpa, Jalisco, and he died during the operation. [19] Reuters counted more than 250 roadblocks across 20 states and reported US intelligence support. [20] InSight Crime put the toll at 62 dead, 25 of them National Guard members. [19]

lenses.local: Ríodoce and Animal Político document the Sinaloa toll behind the national average, and Zeta reports that only 15 of the 76 priority targets in Baja California hold arrest warrants. [3] [18] [21]
lenses.international: Reuters and EFE carry the government's figures and the Mencho raid, and Reuters relays analysts' doubt that the army can fight two cartels at once. [20] [17]
lenses.scholar: WOLA's Stephanie Brewer argues that removing cartel leaders has historically raised homicides and fragmentation, and InSight Crime sees a high risk of CJNG splintering. [7] [19]

sections.title: Cartels earn from extortion, fuel theft and timber, while most priority targets lack arrest warrants
sections.body_md:
Canada's Immigration and Refugee Board, summarising several sources, lists drug trafficking (especially synthetic drugs), extortion, fuel theft, migrant smuggling and money laundering among cartel activities. It says cartels have gained influence over legal businesses, local governments and elections. The Sinaloa Cartel has been fractured since the arrest of El Mayo in 2024, with fighting between the Chapitos and Mayitos factions. [9]

Fuel theft reaches the state oil company. The Rio Times reports that Pemex lost MXN 9.18 billion (US$494 million) to it in the second quarter of 2026. [22] The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime found that officials estimate about half of Chihuahua's timber is illegal, and that in 2023 about 7,000 cubic metres of illegal wood was seized, roughly 0.007 percent of the 886,576 cubic metres produced. That year there were 10 arrests and no convictions. [23]

Armed groups also recruit children. Proceso's cover report of 3 October documents minors recruited or abducted in Jalisco, Michoacán and Veracruz, and notes that legislators have not considered a specific crime of forced recruitment. [24]

Zeta's investigations unit reports that the priority list held by Baja California's security coordination table has 76 names, of which 15 have arrest warrants. By group, it counts 27 Mayiza, 20 CJNG, 17 Arellano Félix and 12 Chapitos targets. [21] International Crisis Group published a report in July 2026 titled "Sinaloa's War of the Splinters", which this draft could not open. [25]

lenses.local: Proceso and Zeta supply the recruitment and arrest-warrant detail, and both rest on their own reporting. [24] [21]
lenses.international: The Rio Times reports fuel theft as a drag on Pemex, with MXN 9.18 billion lost in the second quarter. [22]
lenses.scholar: GI-TOC documents logging and extortion by Sinaloa Cartel factions and CJNG-allied groups in Chihuahua, and notes that evidence of mining companies working with criminal groups in Sonora is unclear. [23]

sections.title: More than 130,000 people are missing, and families do much of the searching
sections.body_md:
The national registry (RNPDNO) holds 67,970 records of missing people from 1 October 2024 to 15 November 2026, including those later found. UnoTV's weekly count says 20,944 of them remain missing or unlocated, and that 217 cases were registered between 9 and 15 November, 141 still unresolved. [4]

The historic total is far larger. Amnesty International, reported by Reuters, counts 133,500 cases at the end of 2025, up 10.5 percent over the year. [26] The National Search Commission lists 133,864, according to Animal Político. [1] UN human rights chief Volker Türk, who visited in April, put it at more than 132,000, called it a crisis and said impunity is victims' main demand. Mexico's government rejected a UN committee report that found crimes against humanity had been and were being committed, and Sheinbaum has said enforced disappearances no longer occur. [14]

Two members of Colectivo Buscadoras Guanajuato argue in an opinion piece that official counts miss families who cannot file complaints and migrants who vanish in transit, and cite more than 70,000 bodies awaiting identification. [27] The Fundación para la Justicia counted 22 searchers killed in 15 years and two currently missing. [1]

In Mexico City, 5,638 people were still missing on 18 September 2026. An Ibero report cited by Proceso found that 53 percent of clandestine graves registered in the capital from 2020 to 2024 were on private property, and families say warrants to enter such homes can wait from six months to five years. [2]

lenses.local: Older investigations by Pie de Página (2022) and Quinto Elemento Lab (2018) show how grave counts by prosecutors and searchers diverge, but this draft found no 2026 piece from either outlet. [28] [29]
lenses.international: Reuters carries Amnesty's finding that disappearances rose in 2025 while murders fell 27.4 percent. [26]
lenses.scholar: Human Rights Watch reports that the UN Committee on Enforced Disappearances opened its first review into whether disappearances in Mexico are widespread or systematic, and that Sheinbaum denied a policy of disappearances. [30]

sections.title: Washington ties trade to security: an indicted governor, terrorist designations and talk of strikes
sections.body_md:
CSIS describes the 29 April US indictment of Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya and nine other current and former officials as the culmination of about 18 months of pressure tying trade benefits to security results. [8] US prosecutors allege Sinaloa Cartel members, including the Chapitos faction, helped secure his 2021 election. Rocha Moya rejects the charges as baseless, and Mexico's foreign ministry said no evidence was attached to the extradition requests. [31] AP reports he stepped aside indefinitely in August. [32]

On force, the record in the sources read is narrower than the rhetoric. In October 2025 the US struck boats in the eastern Pacific and killed 14 people, and Sheinbaum said "We do not agree with these attacks." [33] Reuters says Trump has repeatedly threatened unilateral military action in Mexico. [20] CSIS reports that Mexico allowed US surveillance drone flights but rejected US troops operating inside its territory. [13] This draft found no source reporting a US strike on Mexican soil.

On 10 November Sheinbaum said the relationship had not changed after the US midterms, in which Trump's party lost heavily. She said the US terrorist designation of cartels does not authorise operations in Mexican territory outside agreed mechanisms, and that Mexico amended articles 19 and 40 of its Constitution to limit foreign action. [12] AP describes her line as cooperation without subordination, and says Mexico sent 92 alleged traffickers to the United States between February 2025 and January 2026. [32]

Proceso quotes Brookings scholar Vanda Felbab-Brown arguing that a US military intervention is unviable and that the terrorist designation gives Washington tools to pressure Mexico, including requests aimed at Morena politicians. [24]

lenses.local: Aristegui Noticias reports that Sheinbaum seeks a tariff deal with Trump in December, and Proceso carries the argument against a US intervention. [34] [24]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera and the Los Angeles Times cover the indictment and the boat strikes, and Reuters reports the repeated strike threats. [31] [33] [20]
lenses.scholar: WOLA argues that US pressure, including tariffs and the threat of unilateral military action, pushed Mexico to meet US security demands. [7]

sections.title: The USMCA was not renewed in July, and tariffs on steel, aluminium and cars are the live issue
sections.body_md:
The United States declined on 1 July 2026 to renew the USMCA. The pact stays in force until 1 July 2036 but now faces yearly reviews, and Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the US did not agree to renew it "in its current form." Economy Secretary Marcelo Ebrard says it will last 10 years with an annual review, a reading the Rio Times notes conflicts with Washington's. [22] Chatham House notes that about 88 percent of Mexican exports to the US enter duty-free under the pact, for a weighted effective tariff of roughly 3.4 percent, and argues that annual reviews prolong uncertainty for investors. [35]

The Rio Times lists a 50 percent US tariff on steel and aluminium and 25 percent on many Mexican autos under Section 232. [22] On 12 November Trump threatened to double tariffs unless Mexico stops a migrant caravan, though Texas Public Radio notes it is unclear what legal authority he would use after the Supreme Court rejected his emergency economic powers in February. [36]

Sheinbaum and Trump met for about 20 minutes on 18 November in Shenzhen on the sidelines of APEC and agreed to meet again at the G20 in Florida in December. Ebrard counted 56 bilateral technical meetings. Reuters data cited by Mexico News Daily put goods trade at about US$779 billion in the first nine months of 2026. [37] Sheinbaum said talks are progressing on vehicle, steel and aluminium tariffs. [5]

The IMF estimates growth at 0.5 percent in 2025 and projects 1.5 percent for 2026. It puts the 2025 fiscal deficit at 4.9 percent of GDP and gross public debt at 61.7 percent of GDP. [38] Pemex reported a third-quarter net loss of MXN 10.8 billion and financial debt of US$77.6 billion. [22]

lenses.local: Mexico News Daily and Aristegui Noticias track the Shenzhen meeting and the aim of a December tariff deal. [37] [34]
lenses.international: Reuters reports that Mexico wants lower US tariffs on vehicles, steel and aluminium and that Washington declined in July to extend the pact. [5]
lenses.scholar: Chatham House calls the treaty's continuation the most important result, and the IMF lists security and judicial independence among the constraints on growth. [35] [38]

sections.title: Judges are now elected, Congress favours the ruling party, and the second judicial vote moved to 2028
sections.body_md:
A constitutional reform that took effect on 16 September 2024 introduced direct election of Supreme Court justices, federal judges and electoral magistrates. It cut the Supreme Court from eleven members to nine and abolished the Federal Judicial Council. The first election, on 1 June 2025, filled 881 positions with turnout of 12.9 percent, and the electoral institute found widespread use of voting guides tied to political machinery. [10] Mexico News Daily notes that many judges elected in 2025, including Supreme Court justices, have links to the government or Morena. [39]

A decree published on 2 June 2026 moved the second judicial election from 2027 to 2028, shortened the terms of judges elected in 2025 and restored two Supreme Court sections. [11] The national association of federal judges, JUFED, called the postponement "the clearest confession" that the original design was unworkable. [39]

The same analysis reports that Sheinbaum's first electoral reform bill failed on 11 March by 259 votes to 234, short of the two-thirds needed, after allied parties broke ranks. A narrower version was published on 23 April. [11] On 20 November Morena ruled out seeking consensus with the opposition on the next head of the electoral institute, and Ricardo Monreal said consensus is not a legal requirement. [34]

Human Rights Watch says prosecutors solve roughly one in ten intentional homicides and that around 40 percent of prisoners are unsentenced. [30] The IMF urges prioritising professionalism, independence and accountability in the judicial reform. [38]

lenses.local: Aristegui Noticias reports Morena's refusal to seek consensus on the electoral institute's presidency. [34]
lenses.international: Bloomberg News reported in February, as relayed by Mexico News Daily, that the court system was in disarray and that businesses were increasingly avoiding it. [39]
lenses.scholar: The Inter-American Dialogue argues the reform did not address police investigation and prosecution, where impunity is driven, and that screening committees keep political institutions in control of eligibility. [10]

sections.title: Journalists, searchers and watchdogs face killings, lawsuits and tax pressure
sections.body_md:
UnoTV, citing unnamed press-freedom defenders, counts 10 journalists killed and two disappeared in the current administration: one killed in 2024, seven in 2025 and two so far in 2026. The latest case was Luis Ángel López Valdez, found dead in Poza Rica, Veracruz, on 11 June. Article 19's longer record is 77 journalists killed since 2000 and 33 disappeared between 2003 and 2026. [40]

SIPAZ, summarising reports, says Article 19 documented 451 attacks on the press in 2025, and that the tax authority revoked deductible status for more than 270 civil society organisations in March. It adds that CEMDA recorded 135 attacks and 10 murders of environmental defenders in 2025. [41]

Mexicanos Contra la Corrupción y la Impunidad says the government withdrew its authorisation to receive tax-deductible donations, that it has produced 850 investigations in ten years, and that the government accused its president, María Amparo Casar, of treason. The article carries no government statement confirming or refuting this. [42] On 12 November MCCI's Leonardo Núñez said seven of ten federal contracts are awarded directly and described a pact of impunity. [43]

Türk praised the federal protection mechanism for human rights defenders and journalists as a regional model. [14] Human Rights Watch counted 51 judicial harassment cases against journalists and critics from January to August 2025. [30]

lenses.local: UnoTV, ADN40 and Diario de Yucatán carry the press counts and MCCI's account, and the MCCI claims have not been tested against a government response. [40] [42] [43]
lenses.international: Reuters reports Amnesty's finding that attacks on defenders, journalists and searchers continued in 2025 as protection mechanisms were reduced. [26]
lenses.scholar: Human Rights Watch and SIPAZ compile Article 19 and CEMDA data and give the fullest view of the pressure on civil society. [30] [41]

sections.title: Mexico has become a landing point for deportees, including thousands who are not Mexican
sections.body_md:
AP reports that Mexico received about 12,000 deported foreigners in 2025, mostly Cubans and Venezuelans, according to Sheinbaum, who has not updated the figure since December. Mexico's government has protested the deaths of 17 Mexicans in US immigration custody or during enforcement operations. [6]

WOLA, with two border-region partners, reports that more than 1,100 people a month deported into Mexico are citizens of other Latin American countries. Since mid-April, ICE has rarely deported Mexicans by land and flies them instead, mainly to Villahermosa and Tapachula. Third-country nationals get ten days to stay, and migrants in Tapachula face detention, cannot work legally and risk ransom kidnapping. [44]

Guatemala's president said 2,284 Mexicans deported from the US had arrived there in 2026, and that they were returned to Mexico within 24 hours under an arrangement with Mexico. [6] SIPAZ reports that irregular crossings on the US southern border fell 90 percent between October 2024 and May 2026. [41]

On 10 November more than a thousand migrants left Tapachula heading north, in estimates of 1,000 to 2,000 people. Sheinbaum said no caravan has reached the US border since Trump returned and described her approach as "accompaniment," not repression. [36] Human Rights Watch reports that the asylum agency COMAR received almost 80,000 applications in 2024 and faced budget cuts. [30]

lenses.local: Local sourcing on migration is thin in this draft.
lenses.international: AP and Texas Public Radio report the third-country deportations and the November caravan. [6] [36]
lenses.scholar: WOLA's report with the Fray Matías de Córdova Center and the Kino Border Initiative is the main research source on the human cost of deportations to southern Mexico. [44]

timeline.text: The Chapitos versus Mayiza war inside the Sinaloa Cartel begins.
Constitutional reform introducing judicial elections takes effect.
First judicial election fills 881 positions with 12.9 percent turnout.
US strikes on boats in the eastern Pacific kill 14 people; Sheinbaum condemns them.
Army special forces kill CJNG leader El Mencho; blockades follow in 20 states.
Sheinbaum's electoral reform bill is rejected 259 votes to 234.
US prosecutors indict Sinaloa Governor Rocha Moya and nine other officials.
Decree moving the second judicial election to 2028 is published.
The United States declines to renew the USMCA; yearly reviews follow.
Trump threatens to double tariffs on Mexico unless it stops a migrant caravan.
Sheinbaum and Trump meet in Shenzhen and agree to meet again at the G20 in Florida.
Morena rules out seeking consensus on the next head of the electoral institute; Sheinbaum aims for a tariff deal in December.

scores.coverage_basis: Reuters, AP and EFE file on Mexico often, and this research found wire copy on the Shenzhen meeting, deportations and the Mencho raid. [5] [6] [20] Mexico also has a deep local press and steady output from WOLA, CSIS and InSight Crime. [2] [7] The wire copy seen centres on trade and US pressure, and disappearances appear mostly in local outlets and rights reports. [4]

severity.basis: The government counts 43.4 intentional homicides a day in October 2026, about half the 2024 level, but Culiacán's rate reached 107 per 100,000 in 2025. [16] [3]
More than 130,000 people are missing, and SIPAZ cites at least 15,795 people forcibly displaced in 2025 across 11 states. [26] [41]
Ten journalists have been killed and two disappeared in the current administration, and judges are now chosen at the ballot with 12.9 percent turnout in the first round. [40] [10]
Growth was 0.5 percent in 2025, the deficit 4.9 percent of GDP and public debt 61.7 percent, with US tariffs on steel, aluminium and autos in place. [38] [22]
Homicides are falling on official data while recorded disappearances rose 10.5 percent in 2025 and US pressure on trade and security keeps rising. [16] [26] [8]

parts.basis: The United States links tariffs, an indictment of a governor and terrorist designations to Mexican security, and Sheinbaum, after meeting Xi Jinping, says Mexico wants stronger ties with China. [8] [5]
Mexico was the top US trading partner in 2024 with nearly US$930 billion in trade, and goods trade reached about US$779 billion in the first nine months of 2026. [13] [37]
Cartels traffic synthetic drugs and run migrant smuggling, and Proceso quotes Brookings scholar Vanda Felbab-Brown arguing that they increasingly resemble terrorist organisations. [9] [24]
Mexico receives deportees from the US, including third-country nationals, and migrant caravans form in Chiapas. [44] [36]
Sheinbaum's constitutional limits on foreign action and Washington's terrorist designations test norms on sovereignty and cross-border enforcement. [12] [8]

summary: Mexico matters beyond its borders through trade, drug and arms flows, migration and the precedent of US pressure on a neighbour's security policy. [8] [22] [44]
gi.up: A US strike on Mexican soil, a collapse of the trade talks or a sharp rise in cartel violence after the CJNG succession.
gi.down: A durable trade deal and a USMCA extension, with continued falls in homicides.

gaps: Crisis Group's Report 112 on Sinaloa could not be opened because its site refused the fetch; only its title and report number were seen, so no Crisis Group analysis is relied on beyond its existence.
No 2026 Carnegie Endowment publication on Mexico turned up in searches, so Carnegie is not cited.

The government outlets named in the brief (Canal Once and the Notimex successor, the Agencia de Noticias del Estado Mexicano) were not found in search. One official gob.mx page is cited from its headline only because the fetch failed, and it is flagged state_affiliated.

Local sourcing from Pie de Página (2022) and Quinto Elemento Lab (2018) is old, and no recent output from either was read. Aristegui Noticias was read through a show summary, and Ríodoce and Zeta through one article each. Local sourcing on migration is absent.
No source read reports a US strike on Mexican soil. The only strikes found are the October 2025 boat strikes in the Pacific, and talk of land strikes is threat and denial.
Homicide figures are government data relayed by one outlet each. No INEGI or independent count was read, and the UnoTV registry counts change constantly.
Book years for the two Ioan Grillo titles were inferred from Publishers Weekly review dates, and the page for Blood Gun Money gives only the month.
Podcast and documentary links point to listing pages, and streaming availability was not checked. The Mexican documentary Volverte a ver dates from 2023.
Not covered in this draft: Ayotzinapa, the 2026 World Cup's security effects, Pemex beyond two results, and Sheinbaum's approval ratings.
The CSIS pages are undated or dated by inference, and the Rocha Moya case rests on Al Jazeera, CSIS and AP summaries without the indictment text.

reporters.name: Jorge Carrasco Araizaga
reporters.bio: Wrote Proceso's 3 October 2026 cover report arguing that Mexico is not a failed state but that the state is increasingly constrained in containing criminal groups.
reporters.why: His report covers forced recruitment of minors and the case against a US military intervention, two threads other outlets cover less.
reporters.label: Proceso, 3 October 2026

reporters.name: Ximena Arochi
reporters.bio: Wrote the 20 October 2026 Proceso report on clandestine graves in private homes in Mexico City, based on registry data and five families.
reporters.why: She documents how slow court warrants stall searches when leads point to private property.
reporters.label: Proceso, 20 October 2026

reporters.name: Alejandro Monjardín
reporters.bio: Wrote Ríodoce's June 2026 piece, in weekly edition 1220, on Sinaloa's fall in the Mexico Peace Index.
reporters.why: Ríodoce is a Sinaloa outlet and reports the cartel war from inside the state.
reporters.label: Ríodoce, 16 June 2026

reporters.name: Daniel Medrano
reporters.bio: Wrote the 5 March 2026 Animal Político explainer that counts 2,425 intentional homicides in 17 months of the Sinaloa conflict.
reporters.why: He compares the state prosecutor's figures with those of the newspaper Noroeste.
reporters.label: Animal Político, 5 March 2026

reporters.name: Parker Asmann
reporters.bio: Author of InSight Crime's 23 February 2026 analysis of what comes next for the CJNG after El Mencho's death.
reporters.why: He sets out the possible successors and the franchise structure that makes fragmentation likely.
reporters.label: InSight Crime

reporters.name: Stephanie Brewer
reporters.bio: Wrote WOLA's 4 March 2026 analysis of the Mencho killing and its 1 October 2025 review of Sheinbaum's first year.
reporters.why: She links US pressure, militarised security and disappearances in one frame.
reporters.label: WOLA

reporters.name: David Mora
reporters.role: Senior Analyst for Mexico, International Crisis Group
reporters.bio: Guest on CSIS's Mexico Matters episode of 28 October 2026 on cartels, drones and US-Mexico intelligence cooperation.
reporters.why: He is Crisis Group's Mexico analyst, and the episode covers the limits Sheinbaum sets on US cooperation.
reporters.label: CSIS Mexico Matters

reporters.name: Alejandra Guillén, Mago Torres and Marcela Turati
reporters.bio: Bylined on the 2018 investigation El país de las 2 mil fosas, which counted at least 1,978 graves from 2006 to 2016.
reporters.why: The investigation is the older benchmark against which later grave counts are read. It is dated 2018.
reporters.label: Quinto Elemento Lab

books.title: Los cárteles no existen / Cartels Don't Exist (nueva edición)
books.author: Oswaldo Zavala
books.why: Argues that the cartel enemy may be a discursive construction that shifts responsibility from institutions, and the new edition extends the argument to transnational militarisation.
books.label: Penguin Random House

books.title: A Narco History: How the United States and Mexico Jointly Created the "Mexican Drug War"
books.author: Carmen Boullosa and Mike Wallace
books.why: Traces how US drug prohibition pushed Mexico to act as an enforcer and argues the conflict is not purely a Mexican problem.
books.label: OR Books

books.title: Gangster Warlords: Drug Dollars, Killing Fields, and the New Politics of Latin America
books.author: Ioan Grillo
books.why: Profiles four criminal groups including Mexico's Knights Templar, and the violence they cause.
books.label: Publishers Weekly

books.title: Blood Gun Money: Firearms Trafficking Along America's Iron River
books.author: Ioan Grillo
books.why: Follows how US firearms reach the black market and seized cartel weapons are traced back.
books.label: Publishers Weekly

podcasts.title: Drones, Cartels, and Sovereignty: Inside the U.S.-Mexico Security Cooperation
podcasts.why: Covers cartel territorial control, drones and the limits Sheinbaum sets on US intelligence cooperation.

podcasts.title: The Monster: Forced Disappearances in Mexico
podcasts.why: Follows a father's search for his son in Guadalajara and asks whether the authorities responsible for searching may be complicit.

media.creator: Manu Ureste and Diego Fernández G. (Animal Político)

media.where: Released in cinemas in 2023; current streaming availability not checked.

local_md:
Ríodoce and Animal Político document the Sinaloa toll behind the national average, and Zeta reports that only 15 of the 76 priority targets in Baja California hold arrest warrants. [3] [18] [21]

Proceso and Zeta supply the recruitment and arrest-warrant detail, and both rest on their own reporting. [24] [21]

Older investigations by Pie de Página (2022) and Quinto Elemento Lab (2018) show how grave counts by prosecutors and searchers diverge, but this draft found no 2026 piece from either outlet. [28] [29]

Aristegui Noticias reports that Sheinbaum seeks a tariff deal with Trump in December, and Proceso carries the argument against a US intervention. [34] [24]

Mexico News Daily and Aristegui Noticias track the Shenzhen meeting and the aim of a December tariff deal. [37] [34]

Aristegui Noticias reports Morena's refusal to seek consensus on the electoral institute's presidency. [34]

UnoTV, ADN40 and Diario de Yucatán carry the press counts and MCCI's account, and the MCCI claims have not been tested against a government response. [40] [42] [43]

Local sourcing on migration is thin in this draft.
international_md:
Reuters and EFE carry the government's figures and the Mencho raid, and Reuters relays analysts' doubt that the army can fight two cartels at once. [20] [17]

The Rio Times reports fuel theft as a drag on Pemex, with MXN 9.18 billion lost in the second quarter. [22]

Reuters carries Amnesty's finding that disappearances rose in 2025 while murders fell 27.4 percent. [26]

Al Jazeera and the Los Angeles Times cover the indictment and the boat strikes, and Reuters reports the repeated strike threats. [31] [33] [20]

Reuters reports that Mexico wants lower US tariffs on vehicles, steel and aluminium and that Washington declined in July to extend the pact. [5]

Bloomberg News reported in February, as relayed by Mexico News Daily, that the court system was in disarray and that businesses were increasingly avoiding it. [39]

Reuters reports Amnesty's finding that attacks on defenders, journalists and searchers continued in 2025 as protection mechanisms were reduced. [26]

AP and Texas Public Radio report the third-country deportations and the November caravan. [6] [36]
scholar_md:
WOLA's Stephanie Brewer argues that removing cartel leaders has historically raised homicides and fragmentation, and InSight Crime sees a high risk of CJNG splintering. [7] [19]

GI-TOC documents logging and extortion by Sinaloa Cartel factions and CJNG-allied groups in Chihuahua, and notes that evidence of mining companies working with criminal groups in Sonora is unclear. [23]

Human Rights Watch reports that the UN Committee on Enforced Disappearances opened its first review into whether disappearances in Mexico are widespread or systematic, and that Sheinbaum denied a policy of disappearances. [30]

WOLA argues that US pressure, including tariffs and the threat of unilateral military action, pushed Mexico to meet US security demands. [7]

Chatham House calls the treaty's continuation the most important result, and the IMF lists security and judicial independence among the constraints on growth. [35] [38]

The Inter-American Dialogue argues the reform did not address police investigation and prosecution, where impunity is driven, and that screening committees keep political institutions in control of eligibility. [10]

Human Rights Watch and SIPAZ compile Article 19 and CEMDA data and give the fullest view of the pressure on civil society. [30] [41]

WOLA's report with the Fray Matías de Córdova Center and the Kino Border Initiative is the main research source on the human cost of deportations to southern Mexico. [44]
